blocks.text: Zechariah 9 places sharply different images beside one another: a humble king riding a donkey removes instruments of war and speaks peace to the nations (vv. 9–10), while the later lines speak of prisoners released because of covenant blood, restored abundance, and military conflict (vv. 11–17). The chapter does not flatten these images into a single simple picture. Its promise of release from a waterless pit and of “double” restoration stands alongside language of bows, swords, and divine defense. This tension is part of the chapter’s interpretive challenge. The larger collection in chapters 9–14 is also largely undated and anonymous and differs in framing and dominant forms from chapters 1–8, which helps explain why this oracle begins with its own distinctive announcement in verse 1.
